lead: Every remote sensing image has four limits: spatial, spectral, radiometric and temporal resolution. Spatial fixes the ground size of a pixel, spectral fixes the number and width of wavelength bands, radiometric fixes the number of discrete levels, and temporal fixes the revisit time. These limits decide what a sensor can see and how often. They are used to choose imagery for crop monitoring, urban mapping, disaster response and water studies. Each finer limit is bought at a cost in another.
prereq: You need Chapter 6.4 for platform height, swath and detector arrays, and Chapter 6.1 for wavelength.

sections.h3: Spatial resolution is the ground pixel size

blocks.text: An image is a grid of picture elements, pixels. Each pixel stores a digital number (DN), an integer code for the radiance received from its ground area. Spatial resolution is the ground size of one pixel. A smaller ground pixel size is a finer spatial resolution; 5 m is finer than 30 m. The sensor height and its instantaneous field of view (IFOV) set it.

blocks.where: GSD is the ground sampling distance in metres; H is the sensor height above ground in metres; θ is the instantaneous field of view in radians.

blocks.text: A sensor at H = 700 km with θ = 10 μrad has GSD = 700 000 m × 10 × 10⁻⁶ = 7 m. A larger IFOV or a higher platform gives a coarser pixel.

When one pixel covers two covers, such as field and road, it is a mixed pixel. Its DN is roughly the area-weighted average of the two radiances. The pixel then belongs fully to neither class. Finer pixels reduce mixing but cost data volume and often a narrower swath. The figure shows nine 10 m pixels averaged into one 30 m pixel.

Spectral resolution describes the number and width of wavelength bands. A panchromatic sensor has one broad band and collects much energy. A multispectral sensor has a few bands, for example visible and near infrared. A hyperspectral sensor has many narrow, contiguous bands. Narrow bands help separate covers with similar spectral signatures, such as two crops.

Radiometric resolution is the number of discrete levels used to record radiance. An n-bit sensor gives 2ⁿ levels. An 8-bit sensor gives 256 levels with DN from 0 to 255. A 12-bit sensor gives 4096 levels with DN from 0 to 4095. More bits mean finer steps between levels, not a larger pixel.

blocks.where: ΔL is the quantisation step in radiance units; Lmax and Lmin are the radiance limits of the sensor; n is the number of bits per pixel; 2ⁿ is the number of levels.

blocks.text: A smaller ΔL means higher radiometric resolution. More spectral bands split the incoming energy into smaller portions, so each band has less signal and a lower signal-to-noise ratio unless the sensor is larger or integration time is longer.

Temporal resolution is the revisit time, also called the repeat cycle: the time between two images of the same ground point. A geostationary sensor stares at the same area and repeats in minutes. A polar-orbiting sensor moves in a swath and repeats in days. Wide-swath sensors revisit more often than narrow-swath sensors at the same altitude.

The four resolutions compete. A finer GSD needs a smaller detector footprint on the ground or a longer focal length, which usually narrows the swath and lengthens revisit. More bands divide the same optical energy, so each band is noisier. Higher radiometric resolution increases data volume. Good design picks the combination the task needs: crop mapping wants spectral and temporal detail; a city map wants fine spatial detail.

Ground sampling distance is not the whole story. Real image quality also depends on the modulation transfer function (MTF), which measures how well contrast survives at fine detail, and on signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Only a few universities teach MTF and SNR as resolution measures; see Chapter 6.7 for how resampling changes pixel size.

spec.aria: An array shows nine 10 m pixel digital numbers, four of them bright, above a single 30 m pixel whose digital number is their rounded mean, 37.
spec.title: Same ground, two spatial resolutions (DN values)

examples.question: A 30 m sensor images a 30 m × 30 m block. The same block is seen by a 10 m sensor as nine pixels with digital numbers 10, 10, 10, 10, 70, 70, 10, 70, 70. Find the single digital number of the block in the 30 m image and the fraction of the block that is bright cover.
steps: Each 10 m pixel covers 100 m²; nine cover 900 m², equal to one 30 m pixel of 30 m × 30 m.
The bright pixels are four of nine: 4 ÷ 9 = 0.4444 = 44.4 per cent.
The coarse DN 37 is between 10 and 70, so the 30 m pixel is mixed; it belongs fully to neither cover.
examples.answer: The 30 m sensor records digital number 37, and 44.4 per cent of the block is bright cover.
examples.check:
vals = [10, 10, 10, 10, 70, 70, 10, 70, 70]
n = len(vals)
mean_dn = sum(vals) / n
bright = sum(1 for v in vals if v > 40)
print(float(round(mean_dn)))
print(round(100 * bright / n, 1))

traps: Finer spatial resolution means a smaller ground pixel size. 5 m is finer than 30 m, not coarser.
Higher radiometric resolution means more bits and more levels, not a bigger pixel or more bands.
Spectral resolution is about band number and width, not about how small a pixel is.
A mixed pixel is not a broken measurement; it is the average of covers inside the pixel.
Temporal resolution is revisit time, not the time taken to process an image.

quiz.q: Define spatial resolution in one sentence.
quiz.a: Spatial resolution is the ground area or ground length covered by one pixel, often given as the ground sampling distance.

quiz.q: Why does a mixed pixel belong fully to neither class?
quiz.a: Its DN is an area-weighted average of two or more covers inside the pixel, so it is not the pure signature of either cover.

quiz.q: A sensor is at H = 700 km with IFOV θ = 10 μrad. Find its GSD.
A 10-bit sensor records radiance from 0 to 1.0 W m⁻² sr⁻¹ μm⁻¹. Find the quantisation step.
quiz.a: Levels = 2¹⁰ = 1024, so DN range is 0 to 1023. ΔL = 1.0 ÷ (1024 − 1) = 0.000978 W m⁻² sr⁻¹ μm⁻¹.

quiz.q: Why does adding spectral bands reduce the signal in each band, and what is the trade-off?
quiz.a: A band takes only its wavelength slice of the incoming energy, so more bands split the same energy into smaller portions. Each band has lower signal-to-noise unless the sensor aperture or integration time is increased. The gain is better separation of similar covers.

quiz.q: Why does a finer spatial resolution often lengthen the revisit time?
quiz.a: A finer GSD needs a smaller ground footprint per detector or a longer focal length, which usually narrows the swath. A narrower swath covers less ground per orbit, so the same point is crossed less often and the repeat cycle grows.

quiz.q: An 8-bit image has how many levels and what DN range?
quiz.a: It has 2⁸ = 256 levels, with DNs from 0 to 255.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real image quality is judged by modulation transfer function (MTF) and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), not only by GSD. MTF measures how well contrast survives at fine detail; SNR measures signal against noise. Data cubes from hyperspectral sensors combine spatial and spectral dimensions. Newer small-satellite constellations trade swath and revisit differently. Search for 'MTF remote sensing', 'signal-to-noise ratio imaging spectrometer', and 'spatial spectral resolution trade-off'.
